sentences.text: The animal measured approximately 50 centimeters in total length and had a wingspan reaching up to 70 centimeters.
Its head featured a robust, pointed beak without teeth, which was near triangular when viewed from the side.
While it possessed advanced traits like a short tail with a pygostyle and a bony sternum, it also retained primitive features such as large forelimb claws and a skull with a closed eye-socket.
Hundreds of complete specimens have been recovered, making it one of the most abundant vertebrates in the Yixian Formation.
In a specimen weighing half a kilogram, the primary wing feathers extended to a length of 20.7 centimeters.
This bird was the first early fossil to show preserved pheomelanosomes, although a second research team failed to locate these traces.
Scientists suggested that the presence of medullary bone in a specific specimen indicated it was a female, as this tissue acts as a calcium reservoir for egg production in modern birds.
The genus was formally described by Hou and colleagues in 1995.
The discovery began in November 1993 when paleontologists Hou Lianhai and Hu Yoaming were shown a fossil bird specimen by collector Zhang He.
Researchers suggested in 1999 that the animal was likely herbivorous based on its upward-curving, non-raptorial beak, although no stomach contents were known at the time.
It possessed large fleshy foot pads and curved claws similar to modern tree-dwelling birds, suggesting it may have had a similar lifestyle.
Flight adaptations included a fused wrist, a short tail, an ossified sternum with a keel, strut-like coracoid, large deltopectoral crest, strong ulna, and enlarged second metacarpal.
It may have had a different flight stroke and was likely not capable of flight for extended periods due to its inability to rotate its arm behind the body and smaller sternal keel.
The flight apparatus was more developed than that of Archaeopteryx, with some specimens showing a keel on the sternum similar to that of modern birds.
This species is the oldest flying dinosaur with an almost modern flight apparatus.
In 2016, Luis Chiappe and Meng Qingjin estimated a maximum egg diameter of 23 millimeters based on the pelvic aperture of a large specimen.
In 2007, Gary Kaiser argued that the animal likely nested in tree crevices rather than open nests and that the small egg size suggests large clutch sizes.
A studied female specimen showed evidence of at least three years of growth, indicating an extended development period similar to non-avian dinosaurs.
Small individuals possessed long tail feathers, suggesting that sexual maturity was reached well before the animals achieved their maximum size.
Analysis of fibrous lamellae indicates that early birds possessed rapid growth phases and high metabolic rates, contrary to previous acceptance.
Forty individuals were found on a 100 square meter surface, suggesting entire flocks were killed by volcanic ash, heat, or gas.
Paleontologist Dieter S. Peters compared the bird to the white-tailed tropicbird, noting similarities in long tails, narrow wings, and nesting habits near volcanoes.
Female mate choice may have been efficient if males participated in chick care, such as protecting the offspring.
Hou assigned the genus to the family Confuciusornithidae in 1995.
The recognized species include C. sanctus, C. dui, C. chuonzhous, and C. suniae, with the latter two possibly being synonyms of C. sanctus.
The species C. chuonzhous was named by Hou in 1997 using specimen IVPP V10919, which was originally a paratype of C. sanctus.
The animal lived in China between 125 and 120 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous Period.
Unlike most species found in the Yixian Formation, C. jianchangensis was discovered in the Jiufotang Formation.
Fossils were discovered in the Yixian and Jiufotang Formations and are part of the Jehol Biota.
It is debated whether two paratype specimens belong to C. sanctus because their bones do not overlap with the holotype.

A 2011 statistical analysis suggested that differences in C. dui might be individual variations within C. sanctus rather than distinct species, though the validity remains debated due to the potential loss of the holotype.
